Neonates of the Desert sand scorpion Smeringurus mesaensis emerge from the brood chamber with a total length of approximately 1.6 centimeters [Lb = approximately 1.6 centimeters], a diminutive size that belies their subsequent developmental trajectory. At birth, these first-instar protonymphs exhibit a wet body mass of merely 0.013 grams [Wwb = 0.013 grams], reflecting the limited maternal provisioning characteristic of this arid-adapted species. This combination of modest linear dimensions and negligible mass at the onset of exogenous life imposes a stringent energetic challenge, as the young must rapidly secure prey items to sustain growth and molt progression. Field observations indicate that the gestation period, timed from syngamy to parturition, spans a full 365 days [ab = 365 days] when females are maintained under laboratory conditions at a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This protracted developmental interval within the maternal ovariuterus is among the longest recorded for any North American scorpionid and is interpreted as an adaptation that synchronizes parturition with the seasonal pulse of small arthropod prey in the dune systems of the southwestern United States.

As the post-metamorphic juveniles progress through successive instars, a steady increase in linear body dimensions is observed, culminating in an ultimate total length of 6.9 centimeters [Li = 6.9 centimeters] for fully grown adults. This overall size at senescence is accompanied by a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 2.2 grams [Wwi = 2.2 grams], representing an approximately 169-fold increase in body mass from the protonymphal stage. The growth trajectory, however, is nonlinear; the most pronounced gains in both length and mass occur during the early and middle juvenile instars, when feeding rates are maximized. Comparative data from the congeneric Smeringurus pallidus suggest that this species achieves a slightly larger ultimate size, though the desert sand scorpion compensates with a more robust exoskeletal armature. Reaching the asymptotic body dimensions requires multiple molting events and typically spans several years, with the terminal molt marking the cessation of somatic growth and the full development of the adult telson and pedipalpal chelae.

The onset of reproductive maturity, defined here as the attainment of a fully functional reproductive system, occurs at a total length of 6.3 centimeters [Lp = 6.3 centimeters] and a corresponding wet weight of 1.6 grams [Wwp = 1.6 grams]. These values indicate that puberty is reached only after a substantial portion of somatic growth has been completed, with individuals at this stage measuring over ninety percent of the ultimate body length. The time since birth at puberty has been estimated at 21.5 months [tp = 21.5 months], a figure derived from captive-rearing studies conducted at a stable temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This relatively delayed maturation schedule is typical of slow-growing, long-lived arachnids and is thought to reflect the unpredictable and resource-limited nature of their desert habitat. Once puberty is attained, individuals shift from a primarily growth-oriented energy budget to one that balances continued somatic maintenance with the energetic demands of gametogenesis and mate searching.

Reproductive output in Smeringurus mesaensis is constrained by both the protracted maturation period and the costs associated with producing a relatively small number of well-provisioned offspring. Under optimal laboratory conditions at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the frequency of reproduction is low, with females typically producing a single brood each year [F_R_i = single brood each year]. Each litter comprises 23 offspring [N_R_i = Each litter comprises 23 offspring], representing the maximum reproductive rate for this species. This life-history strategy, characterized by low fecundity and high maternal investment per offspring, aligns with the predictions of the bet-hedging model common among organisms inhabiting unpredictable aridity-prone environments. The energetic cost of gestation, which includes the provision of yolk reserves and the maintenance of the developing embryos over 365 days [ab = 365 days] at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], is substantial and likely limits the capacity for more frequent reproductive events. Males, by contrast, may engage in multiple mating bouts per season, though their indirect contribution to offspring provisioning is negligible.

Longevity records for the species indicate that maximum lifespan in the wild reaches approximately 2135 days [am = approximately 2135 days], a figure that, when converted to years, corresponds to roughly 5.8 years under the prevailing thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This extended life expectancy is consistent with the slow-paced life history of many psammophilous scorpions and is partly attributable to a low basal metabolic rate and effective resistance to desiccation. The combination of a late age at puberty, modest annual reproductive output, and a long adult lifespan creates a demographic profile in which population growth rates are relatively insensitive to short-term fluctuations in juvenile survival. Instead, the persistence of local populations appears tightly linked to the survival of reproductively active adults across multiple years. Senescence-related mortality is gradual, with a progressive reduction in feeding success and locomotor performance observed in the oldest individuals, ultimately culminating in physiological death.
